deposits.genre_observed: Zenodo metadata packet for a philological article on Sappho fr. 31

finds.quote: The distal demonstrative κῆνος ("that man") in line 1 points not to a present rival but to a future reader—the one who will sit "face-to-face" (ἐνάντιος) with the inscribed text. He is "equal to the gods" (ἴσος θεοῖσιν) because he achieves what should be impossible: presence with the dead.
finds.note: Historical-interpretive thesis on what κῆνος in fr. 31 originally referred to.

finds.quote: The second-person addressee (τοι, σ') is identified not with a beloved woman but with the poem itself—Sappho-as-inscribed. The speaker addresses her future archived self. The physiological symptoms are triggered by this imaginative projection: she sees herself being read.
finds.note: Thesis on the original referent of the second-person addressee in fr. 31.

finds.quote: The progression of bodily failures—voice, tongue, skin, sight, hearing, motor control, colour—traces not jealous collapse but systematic dematerialization: the staged withdrawal of everything that constitutes embodied presence, until only the inscribable remains.
finds.note: Thesis on what the somatic catalogue originally traces.

finds.quote: The simile χλωροτέρα ποίας ("greener/paler than grass") figures the speaker's transformation into papyrus substrate. The χλωρός spectrum (green → grey) traces the colour of papyrus in preparation for inscription. The body becomes the book.
finds.note: Thesis on the original sense of χλωροτέρα ποίας (papyrus colour).

finds.quote:
A new reconstruction completes the poem's logic:


ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον· ἐπεί σε, Κύπρι,
καὶ πένητά γε κἄ βασιλῆα δάμασσε·
καὶ πόλεις ὀλβίους ἀπέθηκας ἄφαντον·
    γράμμασι μολπὰν


"But all must be dared; for you, Kypris, have yoked beggar and king alike, and you have cast down even prosperous cities to nothing—let the song survive in letters."
finds.falsifier_quote: Future papyrological discoveries may confirm, modify, or refute this reconstruction. Until then, it stands as hypothesis.
finds.note: Reconstruction of the lost fourth stanza; the deposit names papyrological discovery as its test.

finds.quote: Fragment 31 emerges as the foundational text of lyric self-archiving—a meditation on how voice outlasts the body that speaks it. Catullus 51 is not imitation but instantiation: Catullus IS κῆνος, the future reader the poem anticipated. The circuit completes in every reading.
finds.note: Reception thesis: fr. 31 as foundational text of lyric self-archiving and Catullus 51 as instantiation of its future reader.

finds.quote:
**κῆνος is the future reader.**


The reader sits face-to-face (ἐνάντιος) with the text. The reader hears the "sweet voice" (ἆδυ φωνείσας)—the words, sounded in reading. The reader experiences the "desirable laugh" (γελαίσας ἰμέροεν)—the pleasure the lyric offers.


And the reader, encountering a voice that has outlasted the body that produced it, achieves something that only gods should possess: **presence with the dead**.


ἴσος θεοῖσιν: "equal to the gods." Not hyperbole. Precision.
finds.note: Thesis on the original referent of κῆνος in fr. 31.

finds.quote:
If κῆνος is the future reader, then the second-person addressee—the "you" (τοι, σ') throughout the poem—must be identified not with a contemporary beloved but with the poem itself: **Sappho-as-inscribed**.


The speaker addresses her future archived self. The physiological symptoms that follow are triggered by this imaginative projection. She sees herself being read. She experiences the vertigo of self-exteriorization: becoming, while still alive, the object of a future gaze.
finds.note: Thesis on the second-person addressee as the speaker's archived self.

finds.quote:
This is not a catalogue of jealous suffering. It is a **catalogue of dematerialization**: the staged withdrawal of everything that makes the speaker a living, present, embodied voice.


What fails first is what cannot be inscribed—the living breath, the sounded word, the immediate presence of speaker to hearer. What remains at the end is what can be inscribed: the words themselves, fixed in letters, readable after the voice that spoke them has fallen silent.
finds.note: Thesis that the somatic catalogue is an ordered dematerialisation, not jealous suffering.

finds.quote:
ποία is usually translated "grass," but the word designates wild grasses, fodder, any non-cultivated ground-cover plant—and by extension, **papyrus** (Cyperus papyrus), a sedge.


The comparison is not conventional. Nothing in the Lesbian landscape matches papyrus precisely. Papyrus grew in Egypt and was imported to Greece as writing material from the 7th century BCE onward.
finds.window: Sappho Fragment 31, line 14; papyrus import from 7th c. BCE
finds.note: Lexical-historical thesis that ποία extends to papyrus and the simile names the writing substrate; argued further at 321-324.

finds.quote:
Satisfying all constraints—ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον (attested), Catullus' "kings and cities," the poem's trajectory from embodiment to inscription, Sapphic diction (γράμματα + μολπά attested in fr. 44.33, fr. 147), Sapphic meter:


ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον· ἐπεί σε, Κύπρι,        – u – x – uu – u – x
καὶ πένητά γε κἄ βασιλῆα δάμασσε·        – u – x – uu – u – x
καὶ πόλεις ὀλβίους ἀπέθηκας ἄφαντον·    – u – x – uu – u – x
    γράμμασι μολπὰν                        – uu – x
finds.note: Reconstruction of the lost fourth stanza (no falsifier stated in this deposit).

finds.quote:
**Sappho** (fl. c. 630-570 BCE): Discovers or perfects the operator. Creates initiatory community (thiasos). Encodes technology in poetry.

- 


**Plato** (428-348 BCE): Receives through textual/cultural transmission. Encodes as metaphysics: Forms as telos, Academy as container, dialogues as recruitment, agrapha dogmata as protection. The Ladder of Love (Symposium 210a-212b) is σ_S in vertical projection.
finds.note: Transmission-history thesis: σ_S propagates Sappho -> Plato (Ladder of Love as σ_S) -> Aristotle -> Alexander -> Rome -> Augustine (Conf. 10.27 repeats fr. 31's sequence).

finds.quote: Catullus 51 is not imitation but instantiation. Catullus **is** κῆνος—"that man" who sits face-to-face with Sappho's text, hears her voice across six centuries, and experiences the impossible presence of the dead.
finds.note: Reception thesis: Catullus 51 as instantiation; otium substitution read as recognition of writing's condition.

deposits.genre_observed: philological article on Sappho fr. 31 (journal format, with notes and bibliography)

finds.quote: κῆνος, I shall argue, is the future reader: the one who will sit 'face-to-face' (ἐνάντιος) with the text, who will hear the 'sweet voice' of Sappho's words and experience the 'desirable laugh' of her lyric. He is 'equal to the gods' because he possesses what should be impossible: presence with the dead.
finds.note: Central thesis on the original referent of κῆνος.

finds.quote: Sappho's innovation—if this reading is correct—is to reverse the vector. Rather than the inscribed object addressing the reader, the poet addresses her future inscribed self: the Sappho who will exist as text, who will be encountered by readers not yet born. The physiological symptoms that follow—καρδίαν ἐν στήθεσιν ἐπτόησεν, 'it set my heart trembling in my breast'—are triggered by this imaginative projection. She sees herself being read. She experiences the vertigo of self-exteriorisation: becoming, while still alive, the object of a future gaze.
finds.note: Thesis that the addressee is the speaker's future inscribed self (reversal of epigraphic reader-address).

finds.quote: This is not a catalogue of jealous suffering. It is a catalogue of dematerialisation: the staged withdrawal of everything that makes the speaker a living, present, embodied voice. And the order matters. What fails first is what cannot be inscribed—the living breath, the sounded word, the immediate presence of speaker to hearer. What remains at the end—the colour-changed body approaching death—is what can be inscribed: the words themselves, fixed in letters, readable after the voice that spoke them has fallen silent.
finds.note: Thesis that the somatic catalogue is ordered dematerialisation.

finds.quote: The simile, I propose, figures this transformation. 'I am becoming greener-paler than grass' means: I am becoming papyrus. The speaker's body undergoes the same process that writing substrate undergoes. She is being prepared—bleached, dried, made ready—to receive the words that will preserve her.
finds.note: Thesis that χλωροτέρα ποίας figures becoming papyrus.

finds.quote:
ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον· ἐπεί σε, Κύπρι,
καὶ πένητά γε κἄ βασιλῆα δάμασσε·
καὶ πόλεις ὀλβίους ἀπέθηκας ἄφαντον·
    γράμμασι μολπὰν
```

'All may be dared; for you, Kypris, have yoked beggar and king alike, and you have cast down even the prosperous cities to nothing—song in letters.'

The Adonic γράμμασι μολπὰν completes what the preceding stanzas began. The speaker, having dissolved into papyrus, commits her song to written form. The poem ends not in prayer or resignation but in the act it has been performing all along: inscription.
finds.falsifier_quote: Future evidence may confirm, modify, or refute it. Until then, γράμμασι μολπὰν stands as hypothesis.
finds.note: Reconstruction of the lost fourth stanza against West and d'Angour; future evidence named as the test.

finds.quote: If Fragment 31 is structured around the future reader, then Catullus' translation is not external commentary but instantiation. Catullus is κῆνος. He is 'that man there' who sits face-to-face with Sappho's text, hears her voice across six centuries, and experiences—as the poem predicted—the impossible presence of the dead.
finds.note: Reception thesis on Catullus 51 as instantiation of the future reader.

finds.quote: For archaic lyric: Fragment 31 is the foundational text of lyric self-archiving. It does not merely anticipate future reception; it thematises that reception, making the transition from voice to text its explicit subject. Other archaic poems survive; this one survives about surviving.
finds.note: Literary-historical thesis on fr. 31's place in archaic lyric.
